posters.title: Get down to their level
prompts: Crouch or sit so your eyes are level with theirs before you start talking.
Wait — count a silent 'one, two, three' after you ask something before jumping in with an answer.
Repeat back what they said, adding one or two new words of your own.
Follow their lead — talk about what THEY are pointing at or playing with, not just what you planned to say.

posters.title: Build the sentence
prompts: Add one word they didn't say, rather than correcting what they did say.
Turn a single word into a short sentence and say it back warmly.
Use 'I wonder...' to open up a comment instead of asking another question.
Narrate what you're both doing together, out loud, in simple words.

posters.title: Every child, every day
prompts: Notice the quiet child — make sure they get a one-to-one comment too, not just the chatty ones.
Comment, not just question — children often talk more freely after a comment than after a question.
Give real thinking time — silence is not a problem to fill.
Use the child's own words back to them before adding anything new.

posters.title: Before you turn the page
prompts: Look at the cover together and wonder aloud what the book might be about.
Point to the picture before you read the words — let the picture do some of the talking too.
Pause on a page you both find funny or surprising and just enjoy it together.
It's fine to skip pages, skip words, or go back — there is no single 'correct' way through a picture book.

posters.title: Read it again (and again)
prompts: A much-loved book is worth reading many, many times — repetition is how children learn to love it.
On a re-read, pause just before a favourite part and let the child fill in the word.
Let the child "read" the pictures back to you in their own words.
Notice what makes THIS book a favourite, and look for another one like it.

posters.title: Books are for everyone, everywhere
prompts: A book works just as well on a lap, on the floor, or outside in the sunshine.
Let the child hold the book and turn the pages themselves.
A wordless or almost-wordless picture book is a brilliant chance to make up the story together.
Keep a small basket of books within easy reach, not just on a high shelf.

posters.title: Sing it, say it, chant it
prompts: A nursery rhyme doesn't need a tune — saying it with a clear beat works just as well as singing it.
Add simple hand actions so children can join in even before they know the words.
Slow a rhyme right down for a child who's still learning it, then speed back up.
Say the same handful of rhymes often — familiarity is exactly what lets children start joining in.

posters.title: Make up your own
prompts: Swap the last word of a favourite rhyme for a silly made-up word that still rhymes.
Turn a child's name into a simple rhyme or chant of your own.
Let children choose which rhyme comes next — ownership keeps them engaged.
Celebrate a wrong-but-rhyming guess just as warmly as a correct one — the rhyming instinct is what matters here.

posters.title: Quiet moments matter
prompts: Build a few genuinely quiet moments into the day — listening needs silence to work in.
Name sounds you both notice — 'I can hear the rain', 'that's a car outside'.
Play a quick guess-the-sound game using everyday noises as you go about the day.
Model really listening yourself — children copy an adult who visibly stops to listen.

posters.title: Listening is a two-way skill
prompts: Show you're listening with your face and body, not just your words.
Give a child your full attention for a moment, even if it is brief, rather than a half-turned ear.
Ask 'what did you hear?' after a walk, a song or a story — it's a different skill from just hearing.
Praise careful listening specifically, so children know exactly what they did well.
